title: Sahih Muslim
hookLine: Muslim's Sahih, known for its careful arrangement

cards: A desk, a lamp, and a stack of notes. One saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has reached you along several chains of narrators, each wording it a little differently. One adds a detail.
One gives the whole scene; another, only the saying. So where do they go in your book? Scattered, a piece here and a piece there, wherever each fits a topic?
Or all together, side by side, so a reader can see every version and spot exactly where they differ? One scholar chose the second way, and it's what his book is known for. Today, Sahih Muslim.

teach.b: First, the man. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, from the city of Nishapur. Muslim here is his name, not only his faith.
Tradition says he studied with al-Bukhari and held him in deep respect. Two students of one science, two books with the same name, sahih, sound. Together they're called the two Sahihs.
Second, the arrangement. Al-Bukhari sometimes divided a hadith across his book, a piece under each heading where it proved a point.
Muslim, for the most part, kept a hadith in one place and laid its chains and wordings next to each other.

For a student, that's a gift: you can watch one saying travel down several roads and see the exact place where a word changes. Third, the doorway. Before the hadith begin, Muslim wrote an introduction.
In it he explains why he takes reports only from people known to be reliable, and he warns against passing things on carelessly.
He records a saying of the scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak: the chain of narrators is part of the religion, and without it, anyone could say whatever they liked.

teach.h: THE CHAIN IS PART OF THE RELIGION.
teach.b: Everything from last week, in one line. Fourth, one hadith from inside.
In Muslim's book, the Prophet says that Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but looks at your hearts and your deeds. Hearts and deeds, together.
Scholars have weighed the two Sahihs against each other, and not all of them came down on the same side. This path takes them as a pair.

how: Sunni Muslims study Sahih Muslim alongside Sahih al-Bukhari, and teachers often use its gathered chains to show students how one hadith came down in several wordings.

o: the book of rulings used by every Muslim court of law
a collection of sayings by early Muslims, not the Prophet
the second of the two sound collections, chains side by side

s: Sahih Muslim is a summary of al-Bukhari's book
it's a separate collection, arranged his own way, with each hadith's chains gathered together.
Muslim wrote an introduction about taking reports only from the reliable
and it records the saying that the chain of narrators is part of the religion.
in this book, Allah looks at faces and bodies
the hadith says the opposite: not bodies or faces, but hearts and deeds.

games.q: you've collected one saying through several chains, each worded a little differently. how do you set them in your book?
o: keep one and throw out the rest.
set them all together, side by side.
games.why: that's Muslim's way. a reader can watch one saying travel down several roads and see where the wording shifts.

practice: Let today's hadith land: Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but at your hearts and your deeds.
Recall the last time you sized someone up by how they looked, the clothes, the face, the car, then turn it around: what did you spend on your appearance this week, and what on your heart?
No verdict, just look, the way you'd look at a receipt; if you pray, you can carry this hadith into your next prayer.

wordCard.voice: Sahih Muslim. The second of the two Sahihs, where each hadith's chains and wordings are gathered in one place, side by side. Today's word.

orig.note: here Muslim is a man's name: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj.

carryVoice: Your line: the second sahih. What Allah looks at: hearts and deeds, not faces. Back tomorrow.
